title: P'an Ku: A Taoist Creation Account
subtitle: A later cosmogony and its editorial frame

creation.locator: Chapter III · Cosmogony-p'an Ku and the Creation Myth; Chapter III · Cosmogony-p'an Ku and the Creation Myth, normalized characters 1680-2330
creation.excerpt: His task occupied eighteen thousand years, during which he formed the sun, moon, and stars, the heavens and the earth, himself increasing in stature day by day, being daily six feet taller than the day before, until, his labours ended, he died that his works might live. His head became the mountains, his breath the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder, his limbs the four quarters of the earth, his blood the rivers, his flesh the soil, his beard the constellations, his skin and hair the herbs and trees, his teeth, bones, and marrow the metals, rocks, and precious stones, his sweat the rain, and the insects creeping over his body human beings
creation.note: Quotation from E. T. C. Werner's 1922 English synthesis; it is not a direct translation of the ancient source it discusses.

origin.excerpt: This account of P'an Ku and his achievements is of Taoist origin. The Buddhists have given a somewhat different account of him, which is a late adaptation from the Taoist myth, and must not be mistaken for Buddhist cosmogony proper.

narrativeBlocks.title: P'an Ku shapes Chaos
narrativeBlocks.body: Werner's 1922 English synthesis describes P'an Ku as a figure who chisels the universe out of Chaos. In this account, his work lasts eighteen thousand years.

narrativeBlocks.title: A world formed from a body
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from the cited English edition (whitespace normalized): “His task occupied eighteen thousand years, during which he formed the sun, moon, and stars, the heavens and the earth, himself increasing in stature day by day, being daily six feet taller than the day before, until, his labours ended, he died that his works might live. His head became the mountains, his breath the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder, his limbs the four quarters of the earth, his blood the rivers, his flesh the soil, his beard the constellations, his skin and hair the herbs and trees, his teeth, bones, and marrow the metals, rocks, and precious stones, his sweat the rain, and the insects creeping over his body human beings”

narrativeBlocks.title: The body becomes the world
narrativeBlocks.body: Werner's account says P'an Ku's head becomes mountains, breath becomes wind and clouds, blood becomes rivers, and flesh becomes soil.

narrativeBlocks.title: Do not call this timeless canon
narrativeBlocks.body: Werner identifies this as a Taoist-origin account and notes that he sees no evidence for P'an Ku before the surviving written account. This is a modern synthesis, not a translation of one ancient creation text.

narrativeBlocks.title: The account has a history
narrativeBlocks.body: The story explains cosmic features through the transformation of P'an Ku's body, while Werner's discussion also records disagreement about the figure's historical development.
